title: Indirect discourse and indirect questions

objectives.can: Recognise reported speech with ὅτι, with the infinitive and with the participle, and an indirect question.

explanation.summary: Greek reports what someone said, saw, knew or asked in four ways: a ὅτι clause, an accusative and infinitive, a participle, and an indirect question. In all of them Greek tends to keep the tense and mood of the original words, so the reported clause often looks like the speaker's own sentence.

sections.heading: ὅτι: 'that', and quotation marks
body: After verbs of saying, knowing, seeing or thinking, a clause with ὅτι reports the content: 'they saw that …', 'we know that …'. In Mark 2:16 the scribes ἰδόντες ὅτι ἐσθίει, 'seeing that he eats'. The verb of the clause, ἐσθίει, is a present, the tense of what they saw, even though the main sentence is in the past. English moves the report back to 'he was eating'. Greek usually does not.

ὅτι has more than one job. It can also mean 'because', as the context shows, and it can introduce the exact words of a speaker, like quotation marks. Grammarians call this the recitative ὅτι. In Mark 1:15 the participle λέγων is followed by ὅτι and then the speaker's own words: Πεπλήρωται ὁ καιρός. You can see that the words are direct from the verbs that come next: the commands μετανοεῖτε and πιστεύετε are addressed to the hearers. In John 10:36, ὑμεῖς λέγετε ὅτι Βλασφημεῖς has a second-person verb: 'you say, You blaspheme', and the person is the one addressed. A true report would have said 'that I blaspheme'. Greek does not mark the difference in writing, since the earliest manuscripts have no quotation marks, so editors decide from the sense.

sections.heading: The accusative and the infinitive
body: Verbs of saying and thinking can also take an infinitive. The subject of the infinitive is in the accusative, as for any infinitive with its own subject. In Luke 24:23 the women report angels οἳ λέγουσιν αὐτὸν ζῆν: 'who say that he lives'. αὐτὸν, accusative, is the subject of ζῆν. In Mark 8:27 Jesus asks τίνα με λέγουσιν οἱ ἄνθρωποι εἶναι; Here με is the subject of εἶναι and τίνα is the predicate, also accusative: 'who do people say that I am?'

When the subject of the infinitive is the same person as the subject of the main verb, it is usually not repeated. In Luke 24:23 the first report, ὀπτασίαν ἀγγέλων ἑωρακέναι, has no subject of its own: the women are the ones who say, and who saw.

The infinitive keeps the tense stem of the original statement. ἑωρακέναι is a perfect infinitive: 'to have seen'. The stems follow the rule from the previous lessons: they show aspect more than time, and the time comes from the verbs around them.

sections.heading: The participle
body: After verbs of perceiving, hearing and knowing, the thing perceived may be put in a participle that agrees with its noun in the accusative. In 2 Thessalonians 3:11, ἀκούομεν γάρ τινας περιπατοῦντας ἐν ὑμῖν ἀτάκτως: 'we hear that some among you are walking in disorder'. τινας and περιπατοῦντας are both accusative plural masculine. In Hebrews 13:23, γινώσκετε τὸν ἀδελφὸν ἡμῶν Τιμόθεον ἀπολελυμένον, the participle is perfect: 'know that our brother Timothy has been released'. In Acts 7:12, ἀκούσας … ὄντα σιτία, the participle ὄντα agrees with σιτία: 'hearing that there was grain'.

This use is a small group of verbs. The test is that the participle does not describe the noun but gives the content of what is perceived. Compare 'I heard the singers' (describing) with 'I heard that they were singing'. The line is not always sharp, and grammarians do not agree on every case. Read the sentence, and ask what the verb of perceiving takes as its object.

sections.heading: Indirect questions
body: A question that is reported inside a statement is an indirect question. It is introduced by the question word of the direct question: τίς, 'who', πῶς, 'how', ποῦ, 'where', or by εἰ, 'whether'. In John 20:2, οὐκ οἴδαμεν ποῦ ἔθηκαν αὐτόν: 'we do not know where they have put him'. The verb is an aorist indicative, as it would be in the direct question. In Luke 6:7 the scribes watched εἰ ἐν τῷ σαββάτῳ θεραπεύει, 'whether he heals on the sabbath'. After a verb of asking, wondering or watching, εἰ means 'whether'; elsewhere it begins a condition, 'if'.

Greek keeps the tense of the question. In Mark 15:44, Pilate ἐθαύμασεν εἰ ἤδη τέθνηκεν: he wondered 'whether he was already dead', with the perfect of the direct thought, 'has he already died?'. A moment later he asked the centurion εἰ πάλαι ἀπέθανεν, with an aorist.

Sometimes the mood changes. In Luke 8:9, the disciples asked τίς αὕτη εἴη ἡ παραβολή: the verb is an optative, where the direct question would have the indicative. This is the optative of indirect question, which is found mostly in Luke and Acts, after a past main verb. In Mark 11:18, ἐζήτουν πῶς αὐτὸν ἀπολέσωσιν, the subjunctive carries the question 'how might we destroy him?'.

misunderstandings: Moving the tense back, as English does. In 'they saw that he was eating', Greek has the present, ἐσθίει. The tense is that of the original thought.
Thinking ὅτι always means 'that'. It can mean 'because' and it can open a direct quotation, and only the context tells you which.
Reading εἰ as 'if' after verbs of asking, wondering or watching. There it means 'whether', and the clause is an indirect question.

Reading the accusative in an accusative and infinitive as the object of the main verb. It is the subject of the infinitive: with λέγουσιν αὐτὸν ζῆν, the people say that he lives, and they do not say 'him'.

deeper.heading: Which construction after which verb?
body: Authors choose among the constructions by habit and by the verb. In the New Testament the ὅτι clause is far the commonest way of reporting speech. The accusative and infinitive is less frequent, and the participle is limited to verbs of perceiving and knowing. Classical writers use the infinitive and the participle more freely, and the spread of ὅτι is usually counted among the changes from classical to later Greek. This course does not require you to predict which a given writer will use, only to recognise each when you see it.

examples.analysis: ἰδόντες is an aorist participle, 'having seen', and ὅτι introduces what they saw. The verb ἐσθίει is present, the tense of what they saw: 'that he eats'. The scribes' words to the disciples follow in the same verse.

options: It means 'that', and the present keeps the tense of what they saw
It means 'because', and the present marks a habit
It opens a direct quotation, and the present is a command
It means 'when', and the present is the historic present
practice.explain: After a verb of seeing, ὅτι gives the content: they saw that he eats. Greek keeps the present of the original perception, where English would say 'was eating'.

options: As a mark that the speaker's own words follow, like quotation marks
As 'that' in an indirect report
As a relative pronoun
As 'because'
practice.explain: The words that follow are direct speech, as the second-person imperatives μετανοεῖτε and πιστεύετε show. This is the recitative ὅτι.

The subject of ζῆν: they say that he lives

practice.explain: In an accusative and infinitive the accusative is the subject of the infinitive. The sense is 'they say that he is alive'.

options: 'If', in a first-pattern condition
'Because', giving the reason
'Whether', in an indirect question

practice.explain: After a verb of watching, εἰ introduces an indirect question: they watched whether he would heal on the sabbath. The verb is a present indicative, as in the direct question.

options: The verb is future
The verb is second person: the quoted words are 'you blaspheme', addressed to the speaker
Because λέγετε is passive
Because ὅτι always introduces a quotation
check.explain: In an indirect report the person would shift to 'that I blaspheme'. A second-person verb for the person addressed shows the speakers' own words. ὅτι does not always introduce a quotation.

options: Both are objects of λέγουσιν, and εἶναι is a purpose infinitive
τίνα is the subject and με is the predicate

με is the accusative subject of εἶναι, and τίνα is its predicate: 'who do people say that I am?'
check.explain: With an accusative and infinitive, the accusative is the subject of the infinitive. The predicate of εἶναι is also accusative, so it agrees with the subject.

options: It agrees with σιτία and gives what Jacob heard: that there was grain
It is an infinitive
It is the main verb

check.explain: ὄντα is a neuter accusative plural participle, in agreement with σιτία. After a verb of hearing it reports the content, 'that there was grain'. It is not the nominative singular that would describe Jacob.

reading.why: The questioning of the man's parents: ὅτι clauses (reported and quoted), indirect questions with πῶς and τίς, and a ὅτι meaning 'because', in six short verses.
